newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - US face payrolls propped up by Europe.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - US face payrolls propped up by Europe.

text.p: Robust U.S. jobs growth could undermine Treasuries against Europe in the short-term, but lingering concerns over European currency union should cushion any blow, analysts said on Thursday.
May payroll data on Friday will be keenly watched for indications the Federal Reserve will need to raise interest rates at its July Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting.

If payrolls expand significantly, the initial impact could be harsh, sending the 10-year T-note/Bund yield spread wider. But longer term the U.S. market was likely to gain the upper hand, analysts said.

"Usually it tends to be one market or the other pulling the spread but there are interesting developments going on in both markets at the moment," said Sally Wilkinson, senior economist at Daiwa Europe in London.

"However if talk of a rate rise at the next FOMC comes back firmly onto the agenda and is validated by the payrolls data then the likelihood is we will see some modest underperformance of the Treasuries," she said.

A Reuters poll of economists forecasts U.S. non-farm employment to have risen 219,000 compared with a 142,000 rise in April. The unemployment rate was expected at 5.0 percent compared with 4.9 percent previously. Average hourly earnings were forecast up 0.4 percent, compared with a 0.1 percent fall in April.
Rob Hayward, economic adviser at BankAmerica in London, said there was a risk people were being too hopeful about the data.

"The market is a bit too long after the gains we have seen this week," he said. "There is some risk interest rates will rise in July and certainly a risk they will have to rise at some point and we expect to see long-term yields back up a bit."
At 1217 GMT the U.S. long bond was at 96-22, to yield 6.887 percent, down from 96-19 in Tokyo and 96-24 in New York on Wednesday.
But on a more medium term view, Hayward said the longer end of the market would be stable, even though the short-end might suffer.
He added the European situation would counter much of the risk from the U.S. data.

"The 10-year spread between the States and Germany will be pretty much unchanged," he said. "It is in a range of 80 to 100 basis points...It doesn't look likely that it will change significantly next week."
The 10-year T-note/Bund yield spread was at 93 basis points having widened from 65 in early January.
Wilkinson said the gap could stretch out to 95 after the data provided there was no interesting news out of Germany.

The German government has been scrambling for ways to help Germany join European currency union after it backed down on a plan to transfer profits from a revaluation of the Bundesbank's gold and currency assets to its coffers this year.

"We've got...these big discussions about what happens in terms of the fiscal position in Germany," Wilkinson said. "If we saw tax hikes coming back onto the agenda there, that would provide an interesting backdrop from a European perspective."
Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International in London, said the U.S./German spread was likely to narrow towards 80 basis points.
He said while there was a risk of some short-term damage to Treasuries from the payrolls report, the market was nonetheless well supported.
"In contrast tomorrow it appears we are going to get some very disappointing German unemployment figures," he said.
He said this would raise further doubts about Germany's ability to meet a strict reading of the Maastricht criteria.
"That means the eruo will be relatively soft and that is not good news for Bunds," Edmonds said.
--Deepthi Wickremasinghe, Bonds Unit +44 171 542 4041
